item.title: RBI reiterates listing mandate for Tata Sons, seeks compliance with norms
item.description: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reiterated that Tata Sons must comply with all regulatory requirements applicable to upper-layer non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), including the mandatory ...
item.dc:creator: Subrata Panda
item.content:encoded: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reiterated that Tata Sons must comply with all regulatory requirements applicable to upper-layer non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), including the mandatory stock market listing, in a communication to the Tata group holding company dated November 16. In a letter addressed to Tata Sons’ chief financial officer, the central bank referred to the company’s October 6 communication seeking regulatory guidance to ensure compliance with applicable regulations. The RBI said while Tata Sons had not sought clarification on any specific regulation or guideline, its request appeared to relate to the discussions at the company’s board regarding listing. “In this connection, you are advised to comply with all applicable regulations/ guidelines/ directions, issued by the RBI in respect of NBFCs in the Upper Layer (NBFC-UL), as stipulated in extant regulations/ guidelines/ directions hosted on the RBI’s website, including the requirement of listing by your company,” the letter said. The latest communication reinforces the regulator’s position on the listing of Tata Sons, which has remained unlisted despite the September 30, 2025, deadline prescribed for upper-layer NBFCs. The development assumes significance, coming ahead of Tata Sons board meeting on November 26. The November 16 letter follows the RBI’s September 11 decision to reject Tata Sons’ application seeking voluntary surrender of its registration as a core investment company (CIC). The rejection effectively closed the company’s principal regulatory route to exit the NBFC framework and avoid the listing requirement. Tata Sons had approached the RBI in March 2024 seeking deregistration after repaying all its debt. The company had sought to move out of the regulatory framework applicable to upper-layer NBFCs, which would have allowed it to remain privately held. However, the RBI rejected the application after examining the various aspects of the request and subsequently directed the company to comply with the regulations applicable to upper-layer NBFCs. Tata Sons was first classified as an upper-layer NBFC in September 2022 under the RBI’s scale-based regulatory framework. Entities classified in this category are subject to enhanced regulatory requirements, including mandatory listing within three years of their classification. Under the revised framework, NBFCs with assets of ₹1 trillion or more qualify for upper-layer classification. Tata Sons reported total assets of around ₹2.01 trillion as of March 31, 2026, placing it well above the prescribed threshold. The RBI had also retained Tata Sons in its list of upper-layer NBFCs for 2026-27, published this August, clarifying that its inclusion was without prejudice to the outcome of the company’s deregistration application, which was under examination at that time. Tata Trusts, which collectively control around 66 per cent of Tata Sons, have favoured retaining the holding company as a privately held entity. On the other hand, the Shapoorji Pallonji group, which holds around 18.37 per cent, has favoured a listing as a potential route to unlock value from its investment and facilitate fundraising against its stake.

item.title: CBDT chief says LTCG, STT proposals under review ahead of Union Budget
item.description: In pre-Budget consultations, economists advise against abolishing LTCG tax on equities for foreign investors, while the CBDT examines proposals to rationalise LTCG and STT ...
item.dc:creator: Asit Ranjan Mishra, Monika Yadav
item.content:encoded: Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) Chairman Ravi Agrawal on Monday said the government was examining industry proposals to rationalise long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax and securities transaction tax (STT) ahead of the Union Budget. Any decision would be taken only in the Budget, he clarified. Speaking to reporters after inaugurating the Taxpayers’ Lounge at the India International Trade Fair in the national capital, Agrawal said pre-Budget consultations were underway and stakeholder inputs, including their revenue implications, were being analysed. “Stakeholders are putting forward their views, Budget meetings are going on, and pre-Budget consultations are underway. We will consider the suggestions, and I’m sure you will get to know on February 1. Ultimately, an analysis is being done. Whatever issues have been flagged or points raised by stakeholders are being examined,” Agrawal said. Agrawal also expressed confidence that the government would meet its direct tax revenue target of ₹26.97 trillion for the current financial year (2026-27) despite higher refunds. He said net collection growth was currently about 12 per cent, while refunds were roughly 25 per cent higher than a year ago. “On a gross basis, the collections are quite good. I believe that since we have given substantial refunds till now, going forward, the collections will be better,” he said. Official data showed net direct tax collections stood at ₹14.42 trillion as of November 10, up nearly 12 per cent year-on-year and accounting for about 53.5 per cent of the Budget Estimate. Separately, at a pre-Budget consultation, economists urged the finance minister not to abolish LTCG tax on equities for foreign investors. “Generally, economists were not in favour of an LTCG exemption for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs). While one economist supported the abolition of LTCG, six-seven economists opposed the idea. Those opposing it maintained that FPIs were not fleeing India because of LTCG but because of the lack of an artificial intelligence investment opportunity in India. If LTCG were the reason, they would not be returning, as is evident from the turnaround in the stock market. In the medium term, they are unlikely to find a market as stable as India,” an economist who attended the meeting said. Another economist who attended the meeting said one view raised was whether India could tax capital gains on the basis of dollar valuations, given that foreign investors had made gains in the stock market but lost some of those gains because of rupee depreciation. “Some people also believe that the global norm is to tax investors on the basis of residence. Our tax policy should not be driven by knee-jerk reactions to stock market cycles. There should be stability. The hard-fought reforms should not be undone,” the second economist said. The first economist said more than 20 economists and officials had attended the meeting. “It was very well organised. The process was rigorous and methodical. We have all given our written submissions,” the economist added. The short- and medium-term economic outlook was among the other issues discussed, the second economist said. “The path of fiscal consolidation, the necessity of fiscal discipline, the importance of capital expenditure, the importance of energising private sector investment, the necessity of increasing the savings rate in the economy, and further strengthening the health of micro, small and medium enterprises were among the other issues highlighted at the meeting,” the economist said. Currently, LTCG on specified listed equity securities is taxed at 12.5 per cent on gains exceeding ₹1.25 lakh in a financial year, while short-term capital gains on such securities are taxed at 20 per cent, subject to applicable conditions. In October, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said she was keen to hear stakeholders’ views on LTCG and STT. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum on October 13, she described the debate over these levies and the tax treatment of different asset classes as healthy. She said both domestic and foreign investors had raised the issue but refrained from indicating whether the government would consider any changes, citing preparations for the upcoming Union Budget.

item.title: Rupee flies high in Asia on easing crude oil prices, foreign flows
item.description: The rupee gained 32 paise to close at 93.93 per dollar on Monday, outperforming Asian peers as foreign portfolio inflows into equities strengthened and crude oil prices eased ...
item.dc:creator: Anjali Kumari
item.content:encoded: The rupee emerged as the best-performing Asian currency on Monday, gaining 0.34 per cent against the US dollar, supported by a sharp reversal in foreign portfolio inflows into domestic equities and easing crude oil prices. The domestic currency settled at 93.93 per dollar, compared with Friday’s close of 94.25, gaining 32 paise. It outperformed its Asian peers, with the South Korean won appreciating 0.16 per cent, the Japanese yen 0.14 per cent, and the Chinese yuan 0.08 per cent. Most other regional currencies weakened against the dollar. The rupee opened largely unchanged but strengthened during the session on dollar sales by foreign banks, likely linked to custodial flows, and private banks, possibly on behalf of corporate clients, dealers said. Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have bought $8.5 billion worth of domestic equities so far in November, as of November 12, putting them on course for their highest monthly inflows in six years. They bought another $611 million worth of shares on Friday. The return of foreign equity inflows marks a sharp reversal from the sustained selling seen in recent months. Inflows into the debt segment have also remained positive, albeit at a more modest pace.  The rupee has also drawn support from lower crude oil prices and the continuing impact of the Reserve Bank of India’s foreign exchange measures, market participants said. “The rupee was supported by inflows into equities. In the near term, the rupee could move towards 94.90–95.2 per dollar. The broader appreciation outlook remains intact, with 93.5 and subsequently 93 continuing to be the key downside levels for the rupee,” a market participant said. Axis Bank, in a report, said: “With oil prices now easing, and FPI flows returning strongly in early November, near-term pressure on the currency has further eased.” The rupee’s one-month realised volatility has also declined to around 4 per cent from 6 per cent two weeks ago, indicating an easing in near-term currency fluctuations. However, external pressures, including uncertainty over the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate trajectory and volatility in crude oil prices amid geopolitical tensions in West Asia, continue to pose risks to the domestic currency. Meanwhile, the yield on the 10-year benchmark government security rose 1 basis point (bps) to 7.32 per cent on Monday, compared with 7.31 per cent on Friday. The yield has risen 73 bps so far in the current financial year (2026-27), indicating continued pressure on the bond market even as the rupee strengthened.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Jensen Huang discusses comeback as Nvidia CEO as allies rally support

Jensen Huang discusses comeback as Nvidia CEO as allies rally support The report comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang

Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy that raised questions over exports of the company's advanced AI chips to China | Image: Bloomberg

Reuters 1 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 8:04 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia's chief executive, and has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter.   One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief's return and would try to garner support from the White House.   "Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen," the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang's support.   The report comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours.   Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy that raised questions over exports of the company's advanced AI chips to China. The scandal has plunged the chipmaker into crisis and sent shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
